And it is finished — an accomplished fact, settled once for all at the cross, “in his body of flesh by his death.” Paul presses the sheer physicality of it against every airy spiritualizing: our peace cost God not a word but a body. And the aim of this reconciliation is breathtaking — to present us “holy and blameless and above reproach before him,” the language of an unblemished sacrifice now spoken over persons. This is the believer’s standing in Christ even now (his flawless record reckoned as ours), to be brought to completion on the last Day, when what we already are by grace we shall be in full.

To that promise Paul at once adds a guardrail: “if indeed you continue in the faith…not shifting from the hope of the gospel.” The “if” is real — only a persevering faith is a saving faith — yet the continuing is itself God’s gift: the saints persevere because God preserves them. And the gospel they must hold to is no regional novelty or secret for the initiated; it has been “proclaimed in all creation under heaven” — a public, worldwide announcement — and Paul himself is its minister, a servant entrusted with a stewardship that came down to him “from God.” Indeed the whole section runs on that note: the gospel, the mystery, its unveiling, Paul’s office, and even his strength are all from God; nothing in it ascends from earth.

So Paul can even “rejoice” in his sufferings for them — writing, as he is, from prison. His startling words about “filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions” take nothing from the finished, all-sufficient atonement (the hymn has just declared it complete); they confess instead that Christ is so joined to his church that her sufferings are his, and that the cost of carrying the gospel through a hostile world — a measure of affliction still to be borne — falls now on his body, the church. Paul gladly takes up his share, and bears it “for the sake of his body.”

At the centre of it all stands the mystery. Not a baffling puzzle, but a secret long hidden in the mind of God — veiled through past ages even while it was being announced in promise, shadow, and type — and “now revealed.” The unveiling was God’s own free choice: we did not search heaven out; God came down and told. And he chose to display the riches of this glory among the Gentiles — the former outsiders, the far-off, made the very showroom of his splendour. The treasure, when the secret is opened, proves to be a Person: “Christ in you, the hope of glory.” Not Christ far above, reached by a ladder of mediators, but Christ himself indwelling his people by his Spirit — the present pledge that the story ends in glory. Here is the death-blow to the whole Colossian error: those who have Christ within lack nothing, and need no further initiation to be complete.

This indwelling Christ is therefore the sum of Paul’s preaching: “Him we proclaim” — a Person, not a programme of rules — warning and teaching everyone (the word rings out three times against all elitism) with all the wisdom that is hidden in Christ, toward one goal: “that we may present everyone mature in Christ.” Not flawless, not an elite few, not mere head-knowledge — but every believer grown up, sturdy, and Christlike. And for this Paul toils and agonizes to the point of exhaustion — yet “with all his energy that he powerfully works within me.” Maximum effort and total dependence, held in a single breath: the labour is real and ours, the strength is real and God’s.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Mystery of Christ in You: Union with Christ as the Heart of the Gospel

The phrase “Christ in you, the hope of glory” (v. 27) is the most compressed statement of the doctrine of union with Christ in the New Testament. The mystery that was hidden for ages is not merely that Gentiles would be included in the covenant people (though that is part of it); it is that Christ himself would take up residence in his people — that the indwelling of the Spirit would mean the indwelling of Christ himself in the hearts of those who believe. Reformed theology has always understood union with Christ as the foundation of all soteriological benefits: it is because believers are in Christ that they are justified, sanctified, and will be glorified. And it is because Christ is in believers that they have the living presence of the hope of glory dwelling within them now.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were being told that they needed additional spiritual experiences and esoteric knowledge to be “complete” or “mature.” Paul says: the mystery that makes for maturity is already in you. Christ in you is the hope of glory. The treasure the false teachers are selling is already yours, in a far more intimate and certain form than they can offer. Now: The believer who feels spiritually incomplete, who is seeking a second blessing, a higher experience, a deeper initiation, needs to hear this: Christ is in you. The one in whom all fullness dwells is dwelling in you by his Spirit. The seeking is not wrong; but what you are seeking is already present. Seek to know more fully the one who is already yours.

verseByVerse.quote: And you, who once were alienated and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And you” — the camera turns. Up to this point Paul has been gazing upward, lost in the glory of Christ — the image of God, the Creator, the Head, the reconciler of the universe. Now, with two small words, he swings that whole towering vision round and points it straight at his readers: “And you…” The cosmic becomes personal. It is one thing to say that Christ reconciled “all things” (v. 20); it is another to hear, “and that includes you.” Paul will not let the hymn stay up in the heavens. He brings it down to the actual men and women of Colossae — and to every reader since — and says, in effect: this is your story. Here is what you were; here is what Christ has done. The doctrine of the supremacy of Christ is about to put on your name.

“But I was never a bad person” — how can this describe everyone outside Christ? Before we look at the three dark words Paul uses, we must clear away a misunderstanding, or the verse will seem to fit only gangsters and not decent folk. Paul is not saying that every unbeliever is a monster, or that the kind neighbour and the cruel criminal are equally wicked in every way they could be. They are not. Many people outside Christ are genuinely warm, honest, and generous — better company on a Monday than many a churchgoer. So how can “alienated, hostile, doing evil” describe the pleasant man next door? Because Paul is not measuring people against each other; he is measuring them against God. The question is not “is he nicer than his neighbour?” but “is his life turned toward his Maker, or away from him?” And every life outside Christ, however charming, is a life lived with its back to God — running its own affairs, however decently, as though the One who made it and owns it were not there. That is the condition Paul is describing, and it fits the respectable man and the criminal alike. They are not equally far down the road, but they are on the same side of the one line that finally matters: outside Christ, with their backs to God. Now look at the three things Paul says that condition involves.

“Alienated” — cut off, and from whom? The word (apēllotriōmenous) means estranged, made a stranger, shut out from a belonging that ought to be yours. From whom? From God. Man was made for fellowship with his Maker, to walk with him as Adam walked in the garden in the cool of the day. Sin shattered that. We did not simply drift apart from God the way old friends lose touch; we were alienated — a real estrangement, a relationship broken off, “separated from the life of God” (Eph. 4:18), “having no hope and without God in the world” (Eph. 2:12). And mark Paul’s word “once”: for the believer this is past tense, a country he has left for good. But it is the present address of every soul that has not yet come to Christ. cf. Isa. 59:2.

“Hostile in mind” — what does this mean? Here is the deeper trouble. The estrangement is not a sad accident or a mere distance; underneath it lies enmity — and Paul locates it “in the mind” (tē dianoia), in the very seat of our thinking and willing. This does not mean every unbeliever consciously hates God or shakes a fist at heaven; most never give him a thought. It means something more settled and more serious: the natural mind is set against God’s rule — it will not have him on the throne, will not bow to his claims, instinctively resists being governed. “The mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God’s law; indeed, it cannot” (Rom. 8:7). The polite indifference of the respectable man and the open scorn of the scoffer are two faces of the same enmity: a mind that has quietly pushed God off the throne and seated itself there instead. cf. Rom. 5:10.

“Doing evil deeds” — the root bears its fruit. Paul moves from the inside outward: alienation (a broken relationship), then hostility (a set of the mind), and now deeds — the works the inner condition produces. The enmity does not stay hidden in the head; it walks out into the life. And notice the logic of the chain: the deeds are the symptom, not the disease. We are not alienated because we do wrong; we do wrong because we are alienated. “Evil” here, too, must be read God-ward: it is not only the obvious sins, but every deed — even the kind and respectable ones — done without reference to God, for self rather than for him, springing from a heart that does not love him. A good act done in the service of a dethroned God is still part of a life in revolt. That is why even our righteous deeds, Isaiah says, can be “like a polluted garment” (Isa. 64:6) — not because kindness is worthless to our neighbour, but because it is offered to God by a heart still turned away from him.

What did that old life look like — for Old Joe? Think of the most decent man on Old Joe’s old street — a thoroughly good neighbour. He paid every bill, kept his garden tidy, lent out his ladder, never robbed a soul, and would have been offended to be called anything but a good man. Ask him about God and he’d have said cheerfully, “I’m not religious — I just get on with my life and do no harm.” And there, in that one sentence, is the whole of v. 21. He was not raging against heaven; he simply ran his own little kingdom from his own front room, with himself on the throne and his Maker nowhere in his thoughts — alienated. His settled assumption that his life was his own to run, God’s claims quietly set aside, was the hostile mind wearing a friendly face. And every tidy, harmless day he lived for himself rather than for the God who gave him breath was, in heaven’s reckoning, part of a life lived the wrong way round — the evil deeds, however pleasant they looked from the pavement. That was Old Joe once. That is every one of us outside Christ: not always wicked by the world’s measure, but always turned away by God’s.

And then comes the most beautiful word in the verse — the next one. “But now…he has reconciled” (v. 22). Paul paints the old life this dark for one reason: so that the grace of the next line will blaze all the brighter. The alienated are brought home; the hostile are made friends; the doers of evil are one day presented “holy and blameless.” Keep the darkness of v. 21 in view, and the “but now” of v. 22 will never lose its wonder. cf. Eph. 2:12–13; Titus 3:3–5.

verseByVerse.quote: he has now reconciled in his body of flesh by his death, in order to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“He has now reconciled” — and notice who did it. Hold v. 22 against v. 21 and the turn is dazzling. Once alienated — now reconciled. One word, “now,” marks the great divide of a life: the enmity is over, the estrangement is healed, the stranger is brought home. And mark the grammar, because everything hangs on it. Paul does not write “you have reconciled yourselves,” or “you climbed your way back to God.” The subject is he — God, in Christ. The offended party is the one who makes peace. We brought nothing to the table but the very hostility that needed reconciling; God did all the rest. This is grace with no ladder in it: not God meeting us halfway, but God crossing the whole distance to fetch his enemies home. cf. 2 Cor. 5:18–19; Rom. 5:10.

And it is finished. “He has reconciled” — the verb points to a completed act, a thing already done and done for good. Reconciliation is not a process you nurse along, nor a probation you must keep passing, nor a peace that could lapse if you slip. It was accomplished at the cross, full and final, when the Son cried, “It is finished” (John 19:30). The cosmic peace Paul announced in v. 20 — “making peace by the blood of his cross” — is here handed to the believer as an accomplished fact with his own name on it. Old Joe does not wake each morning to re-earn God’s welcome; he wakes already reconciled, and lives the day from a peace that is settled, not toward one he is still trying to win. This is the very heart of the letter’s quarrel with the false teachers: peace with God is achieved, not assembled by rule-keeping and ladder-climbing.

“In his body of flesh by his death” — why is Paul so insistent on the physical? He piles up the words deliberately: not merely “in his body,” but “in his body of flesh,” and not merely “by Christ,” but “by his death.” Two reasons drive the emphasis. First, the false teachers were spiritualizers: they prized mystical ascent, secret knowledge, and angelic mediation, and would have found something crude, almost embarrassing, in the idea that salvation came through a bleeding human body on a Roman cross. Paul will have none of it. He nails reconciliation to flesh and blood and a real corpse — no airy spirituality that floats free of the cross. Second, it reaches back to the hymn: the One in whom “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (2:9) saved us in a real human body. He had to become flesh in order to die for flesh; God as pure spirit cannot bleed. The phrase “body of flesh” also marks out his mortal, crucifiable body — the body that could be scourged and pierced — as the place where the work was done. Our peace did not cost God a word; it cost him a body. cf. Heb. 10:10.

“To present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him” — what is Paul describing? Here is the purpose of the reconciliation — not merely to spare you, but to present you. The word (paristēmi) is the language of bringing someone forward and setting them in place — a bride led to the altar, an offering set before God. And the three words pile up the glory: holy (set apart, belonging wholly to God); blameless (amōmos — without blemish, the very word used of a sacrificial lamb fit for the altar, not a spot or defect on it); above reproach (anenklētos — a courtroom word meaning unaccusable, against whom no charge can be laid, no accusation made to stick). And all of it “before him” — in God’s own presence, under his searching gaze, where no flaw could hide.

“But I never feel holy, blameless, or above reproach — how can this be me?” Old Joe knows his own heart too well to recognise himself in those three shining words, and he is honest to say so. Two truths set him free. First, this is your standing, not your feeling. It is not a description of how holy you have managed to become; it is a verdict about how God now sees you in Christ. When Jesus reconciled you, his own flawless record was credited to your account — counted as yours, as truly as if you had lived it — while your sin was counted his and paid for at the cross (this is what is meant by being given a righteousness that is not our own; 2 Cor. 5:21). So “above reproach” is the literal truth of your case in heaven’s court right now: the charge sheet has been torn up, and not one accusation can be made to stick. “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? …Christ Jesus is the one who died” (Rom. 8:33–34). When God looks at Old Joe in Christ, he does not see a patchy, stumbling man hoping to do better; he sees his Son’s own holiness wrapped around him, and pronounces him blameless — not because Joe feels it, but because Christ is it.

Second, what you are now by reckoning, you will one day be in full. Paul says “to present you” — and there is a day coming when Christ will lead his people forward and set them faultless before the throne of glory with great joy (Jude 24; Eph. 5:27). The holiness reckoned to you now will then be finished in you completely; the feeling will at last catch up with the fact. So Old Joe’s sense of falling short is not a contradiction of this verse — it is simply the gap between his standing (already perfect in Christ) and his experience (still being made holy day by day). And here is the rest for a weary conscience: the closing of that gap does not rest on Joe’s grip on God, but on God’s grip on Joe. The same One who reconciled him will be the One to present him — and he does not begin a work he fails to finish (Phil. 1:6). The verse does not ask Old Joe to feel blameless; it invites him to believe that he is — and to live tomorrow as a man already brought home.

verseByVerse.quote: if indeed you continue in the faith, stable and steadfast, not shifting from the hope of the gospel that you heard, which has been proclaimed in all creation under heaven, and of which I, Paul, became a minister.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“If indeed you continue in the faith” — does my salvation hang on a thread, then? The little word “if” can land on a tender conscience like a cold draught. Paul has just promised, gloriously, that Christ will present the believer “holy and blameless” (v. 22) — and now, in the same breath, he adds a condition: if you continue. Is it all contingent after all? Could a man be reconciled today and lost tomorrow if his grip slips? We must not soften the “if”: it is real, not a figure of speech. Paul means exactly what he says — the people who will be presented holy are the people who keep believing to the end. A faith that finally and totally collapses and walks away was never the living thing it seemed (1 John 2:19, “they went out from us, but they were not of us”).

But look closer, and the cold draught turns to warm assurance. Yes, salvation rests on a faith that continues — but the continuing is not a weight laid on Old Joe’s own strength, as though he must grit his teeth and hope his grip holds out for fifty years. The continuing is itself God’s gift and God’s work. The same God who reconciled him has pledged to keep him: “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion” (Phil. 1:6); “my sheep…no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28–29); they are “kept by the power of God through faith” (1 Pet. 1:5). So perseverance and preservation are two sides of one coin: the saints persevere because God preserves them. Picture a climber roped to an expert guide on the mountain. He must keep climbing — “if you keep climbing, you will reach the summit” is perfectly true, and his effort is real. But he is roped to a guide who will not let him fall, and when his boot slips on the loose rock — as it will — the rope holds. His safety never rested on the strength of his own fingers, but on the rope and the One holding it. Old Joe’s continuing is real, and required, and his own — and underneath it, holding it up, is the faithfulness of God. So the “if” is not meant to torment him with “have I enough faith to make it?” It is a summons to keep going — and, for the one who keeps clinging to Christ through all his stumbles, the very proof that God is holding him. cf. Jude 24–25; John 6:39.

“Stable and steadfast, not shifting from the hope of the gospel” — what kind of continuing? Paul reaches for two pictures. “Stable” (themeliōmenoi) is a building word — founded, set on a foundation that will not give way. “Steadfast” (hedraioi) means firmly seated, settled, immovable, like something bolted down. Then the warning note: “not shifting” — not being budged, drifting, or carried off “from the hope of the gospel that you heard.” This is aimed straight at Colossae’s danger. The false teachers were trying to move them — off the simple gospel of grace and onto some newer, “deeper” teaching dressed up as spiritual progress. Paul’s charge is, in effect: stay put. Do not drift from the message you first believed. And notice the anchor — the “hope of the gospel”: the gospel carries a hope at its heart, the glory laid up for you (he will call it “Christ in you, the hope of glory,” v. 27), and steadfastness means keeping your eyes fixed there and refusing to be talked off it. The mark of the genuine article is not that it is forever chasing the newest thing, but that it stays anchored to the old, sufficient gospel. cf. Eph. 4:14; Heb. 6:19.

“Proclaimed in all creation under heaven” — what Paul did and did not mean. He did not mean that every single person on earth had already heard the gospel, that the message had reached every village on every continent and the Great Commission was finished. That plainly was not so. This is the warm, sweeping language of a man describing something universal and unstoppable, not filing a statistical report. What Paul did mean is that the gospel is no regional novelty, no secret teaching for a chosen few — it is a public, world-wide announcement, going out and bearing fruit across the known world (as he has already said, v. 6). And that is a pointed contrast. The false teaching prized hidden knowledge for an inner circle of initiates; the gospel is the very opposite — openly preached to all creation under heaven. So the Colossians should feel the absurdity of being lured away: why trade a place in a worldwide, God-driven gospel for a little local secret society? The novelty is the heresy; the gospel is the universal, catholic faith. cf. Col. 1:6; Mark 16:15.

“Of which I, Paul, became a minister” — why mention himself here? Three quiet purposes. First, it puts his own weight behind the message: the apostle himself is bound to this gospel — the very one they heard from Epaphras — not to some rival or “improved” version. Stay with what Paul serves. Second, mark the word he chooses: minister (diakonos, servant) — not master, not lord, not the self-styled expert with the secret. Paul did not invent the gospel and does not own it; he serves it — the same humble word he used of faithful Epaphras (v. 7) — which is itself a quiet rebuke to teachers who lord superior knowledge over the flock. Third, it is a hinge: with these words Paul turns from the gospel itself to his own ministry of it, the very theme he now opens up in vv. 24–29 — his stewardship, his suffering, and his labour to present everyone mature in Christ.

What was Paul after in this verse — why write it at all? It is the guardrail set right at the cliff-edge of grace. Having promised that Christ will present them holy and blameless (v. 22), Paul will not let that glorious assurance curdle into careless presumption — so he adds, at once, “if indeed you continue.” The verse holds together two things that anxious hearts tend to tear apart: real security and real perseverance. He writes it, first, to steady a church under pressure — keep going, stay founded, do not drift; second, to assure them that the gospel they hold is the real, worldwide, apostolic faith, not worth swapping for any novelty; and third, to anchor their confidence not in themselves but in the gospel and the God who stands behind it. In a single sentence Paul turns the soaring doxology of vv. 15–22 toward the hard pastoral work of the chapters to come: hold fast to Christ, for in him — and nowhere else — you are complete (cf. Col. 2:6–7).

verseByVerse.quote: Now I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake, and in my flesh I am filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of his body, that is, the church,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Now I…” — the focus turns to the servant. Paul has been lifting our eyes to the gospel and to the Christ at its centre; in v. 23 he slipped in, almost in passing, that he “became a minister” of it. Now he opens that up. The “I” comes to the front, and from here through 2:5 Paul speaks personally of his own ministry — his suffering, his stewardship, his toil — on behalf of churches he has never even met (2:1). And we must not forget where he is as he writes these lines: in chains (“remember my chains,” 4:18; cf. 4:3). The man penning this soaring praise of the supremacy of Christ is doing so from a prison cell. That is the setting for what he now says about suffering and joy.

“I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake” — what sufferings, and how can he rejoice? Paul’s life as an apostle was one long catalogue of hardship — floggings, stonings, shipwreck, hunger, sleepless nights, and prison after prison (2 Cor. 11:23–28). The “sufferings” here are the cost of carrying the gospel to the Gentiles, the Colossians among them. And his rejoicing is no grim masochism, as though pain were a good thing in itself. He rejoices for three reasons folded into the verse. First, the suffering is “for your sake” — it is fruitful, it serves the church, it is spent on people he loves; a wound borne for those you love is a wound you can bear gladly. Second, to suffer for Christ is to be drawn into fellowship with Christ himself — “that I may…share his sufferings” (Phil. 3:10); the apostles went out “rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name” (Acts 5:41). Third, his joy rests not in the pain but in what the pain is accomplishing. The joy is Christ-centred and others-centred: Paul can rejoice in a cell because through it the gospel runs free and a church is being built. cf. 2 Cor. 1:5–7.

“Filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions” — one of the hardest phrases Paul ever wrote. We must begin by saying firmly what it cannot mean. It cannot mean that Christ’s atoning sufferings were somehow insufficient, that his death on the cross left a deficit for Paul (or the saints, or anyone) to make up. The letter has just declared the very opposite: the fullness of God dwelt in him, he made peace “by the blood of his cross” (1:19–20), and he “has now reconciled” us — finished, complete (1:22). Christ’s sin-bearing, wrath-absorbing suffering lacks nothing; to it not one drop can ever be added. “It is finished” (John 19:30). Whatever Paul means, he does not mean that.

What, then, does it mean? The key is to see that the New Testament speaks of two kinds of suffering bound up with Christ. There is his atoning suffering — the once-for-all, unrepeatable work of the cross, which we receive but never share. And there are his ongoing afflictions in and through his suffering people as the gospel advances in a hostile world — for Christ is so joined to his church that to strike the church is to strike him: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4). The risen Christ no longer suffers in his own body in heaven; but he goes on suffering in his members on earth as his mission rolls forward. There is, as it were, a measure of such affliction still to be borne before the end — a quota not yet filled — and Paul gladly takes up his share of it. When he is beaten and imprisoned for preaching Christ, the afflictions of Christ’s mission are being “filled up” in his own flesh. He is not adding to the atonement; he is taking his portion of the cost of spreading what the atonement secured.

“For the sake of his body, that is, the church.” Here is what turns the hardship into joy. Paul’s suffering is not random or wasted; it is for the church — the very means by which the gospel reaches them and they are built up. His chains are productive: through them the word runs, churches are planted, believers are strengthened. And what was true of the apostle holds, in its measure, for every believer since. When a Christian today bears loss, scorn, or hardship for Christ’s sake or the gospel’s, it is not meaningless misfortune; it is a share in the afflictions of Christ, counted into the great work he is doing in the world, and borne for the good of his people — therefore, however painful, never wasted. The cell where Paul sat was not a dead end; it was a pulpit. cf. Phil. 1:12–14; 2 Cor. 4:10–12.

verseByVerse.quote: of which I became a minister according to the stewardship from God that was given to me for you, to make the word of God fully known, the mystery hidden for ages and generations but now revealed to his saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“A minister according to the stewardship” — what is Paul saying about his role? Again Paul calls himself a minister (diakonos, servant) — in v. 23 a servant of the gospel, here a servant of the church. And he describes his office with a homely word: stewardship (oikonomia). A steward in that world was the trusted manager of a great household — not the owner, but the servant put in charge of the owner’s estate, entrusted with the keys and the storeroom, whose task was to dispense the master’s provisions to the family at the proper time. Three things follow. The steward does not own what he handles — the gospel is not Paul’s to alter or sell; it is God’s, placed in his hands. The steward did not appoint himself — he was put in charge. And the steward must one day give account. So Paul does not stand over the Colossians as a lord with his own message; he stands among them as a trusted servant dispensing what belongs to Another — “given to me for you,” the whole trust handed over for their benefit, not his own prestige. cf. 1 Cor. 4:1–2.

“From God” — and there is the wonder. Where did this stewardship come from? Paul will not let it be missed: it is the stewardship “from God…given to me.” He did not volunteer for the office, invent the message, or earn the trust — it came down to him. And once you see it, you cannot stop seeing it through this whole passage: the gospel is God’s, the mystery is God’s, the revealing of it is God’s doing, the stewardship is God-given, the office is God-appointed — and even the strength to carry it out is “his energy that he powerfully works within me” (v. 29). From first to last, everything in these verses descends from heaven; not one thread of it ascends from earth. Paul contributes nothing of its origin; he is a pair of hands holding a trust that is wholly from above. And so it is with the whole of salvation: it is all of God. The same grace that reached down and made a persecutor into a steward is the grace that reached down for Old Joe. Nobody climbs up to this; it comes down. cf. Eph. 3:7–8; 1 Cor. 15:10.

“To make the word of God fully known” — which “word,” and why “fully”? What is the “word of God” Paul is charged to dispense? Not, in the first place, the Bible as a finished book on a shelf — the New Testament was still being written. In Paul’s mouth “the word of God” is normally the gospel message, the word God has spoken about his Son (he has already called it “the word of the truth, the gospel,” v. 5; cf. 1 Thess. 2:13). So the immediate sense is the gospel — though it is no less than God’s own word, carrying his authority, and it stands in perfect harmony with all of Scripture, which is equally God’s word. And “fully known” (plērōsai, to fill up, to complete) carries a double force. Paul preaches the gospel completely — the whole counsel of God, nothing held back, no part edited out to please his hearers (cf. Acts 20:27); and he carries it to its full reach — out to the Gentiles, to the ends of the earth, until the word has run its appointed course. Mark the rebuke folded inside this: the false teachers wanted to add to the gospel, as though it were lacking. Paul says the gospel is already full; his task is not to supplement it but to declare the whole of it and spread it everywhere. Old Joe needs no secret extra — he has the complete word.

“The mystery” — what does Paul mean? Here we must clear away a modern habit of mind. In the Bible a “mystery” (mystērion) is not a baffling puzzle for clever people to crack, nor something that stays murky and unknowable. It is a secret once hidden in the mind of God and now openly told — a truth no one could ever have worked out by reason or research, which God has chosen to bring out into the light. The content of this particular mystery Paul gives in the very next breath: “Christ in you, the hope of glory” (v. 27) — the astonishing plan, hidden for ages, that Christ would be proclaimed among the Gentiles and would dwell by his Spirit in all who believe, Jew and Gentile together in one body (cf. Eph. 3:4–6). And note the deliberate irony against the Colossian error: the false teachers traded in secret knowledge for an inner ring of initiates. Paul takes their favourite kind of word — “mystery” — and turns it inside out: God’s great secret is not hoarded for the few; it is published to all.

“Hidden for ages and generations” — yet it was announced all along. The mystery was “hidden from ages and generations” — concealed through all the long stretches of past history; God held his full plan close. And yet — here is the delicate truth — it was not absent from the Old Testament. It was there the whole time, but veiled: announced in promise, sketched in shadow, foretold in type. The seed-promise that the woman’s offspring would crush the serpent (Gen. 3:15); the pledge to Abraham that in him all the nations would be blessed (Gen. 12:3); the Servant set as “a light for the nations” (Isa. 49:6) — the lines were all on the canvas. But they lay in shadow. The Old Testament saints held the promises without yet seeing clearly how they would converge in a crucified and risen Messiah who would live inside his people, Jew and Gentile alike. It is like a letter sealed and addressed to you, lying on the table for generations — the message real and waiting, but unread until the day it is opened; or a picture whose central figure cannot be made out until the light is finally turned up. Announced, yes — and still hidden — until Christ came and drew back the curtain. cf. Rom. 16:25–26; 1 Pet. 1:10–12; Luke 24:27.

“But now revealed to his saints” — God unveiled it; we did not find it out. Feel the force of the word “revealed,” and that it stands in the passive: the mystery was revealed. By whom? By God. And this is the wonder that should stop Old Joe in his tracks. The deepest truth in the universe was not unearthed by philosophers, not discovered by the spiritually advanced after long climbing, not cracked open by the clever. It was unveiled from above, freely, by a God who chose to make himself known. Man’s religion is forever a ladder — reaching up, searching out, ascending to find God. The gospel runs the other way: God comes down and tells. We did not find him out; he made himself known. There is grace even in the knowing. And to whom? “To his saints” — and that word matters twice over. First, “saints” (hagioi, holy ones) is the New Testament’s ordinary name for all believers, not a spiritual elite — the plain truth aimed squarely at a heresy that reserved its secrets for an inner circle. The mystery is for the whole household of faith, the humblest believer included; Old Joe is a “saint,” and this is for him. Second, though it is now preached openly to all, it is truly received only by those to whom God grants eyes to see — for “the natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God…they are spiritually discerned” (1 Cor. 2:14). The same Lord who unveiled the secret also opens the heart to welcome it. So this is not a truth the saints were sharp enough to grasp; it is one their God was gracious enough to give. “I thank you, Father…that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children” (Matt. 11:25). cf. Eph. 3:5; 1 Cor. 2:9–10.

verseByVerse.quote: To them God chose to make known how great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“God chose to make known” — it was his choosing. Before we reach the glory of what is revealed, Paul wants us to feel that it was revealed at all — and why. “God chose” (he willed it; it was his good pleasure) to make it known. The unveiling was not owed to anyone, not earned, not inevitable. God could have kept his secret locked in his own heart through all eternity and wronged no one. Instead he chose to tell. Sit with that. The same sovereign will that chose Abraham out of Ur, that chose Israel out of all the nations, has now chosen to fling open his deepest secret — and to fling it open to outsiders and rebels. That God should want to share the hidden riches of his glory with the likes of us is a wonder before it is ever a doctrine. The knowing is not our achievement; it is his gift, flowing from nothing in us and everything in him. cf. Matt. 11:26 (“such was your gracious will”); James 1:18.

“Among the Gentiles” — why does Paul point there? Because that is the scandal and the marvel at the very heart of the mystery. To a Jewish mind the Gentiles were the outsiders — the far-off, the unclean, “strangers to the covenants of promise…having no hope and without God in the world” (Eph. 2:12). That God’s richest glory would be put on display among them — that the nations once shut out would become the very showroom of his splendour — was the part no one saw coming (Eph. 3:6). And Paul says it to the Colossians because they are those Gentiles. He is telling them, in effect: this is about you. You who were far off, you who had no claim, are now the place where God chose to unveil the wealth of his glory. It is the death of every spiritual snobbery: God delights to show his greatest riches not among the religious insiders but among the unlikeliest outsiders. cf. Eph. 2:11–13; Rom. 15:9–12.

“The riches of the glory of this mystery” — what is Paul reaching for? Notice how the words pile up — not just “the mystery,” but its glory; not just its glory, but the riches of its glory; and Paul even asks how great those riches are. He is straining language to its limits, the way a man does when the thing he is describing is too large for words. “Riches” speaks of inexhaustible, overflowing wealth; “glory” of the sheer weight and radiance of God’s own splendour. So this once-hidden secret is no dry fact to be filed away; it is a treasure of immeasurable, dazzling worth. And what is the treasure? Paul does not leave us guessing — the next words name it. The boundless wealth of glory turns out to be a Person.

“Christ in you, the hope of glory” — the mystery in four words. Here is the treasure, and it is staggering in its simplicity: Christ in you. Not Christ far above you, reached only by climbing a ladder of angels and rituals — the very thing the false teachers were selling. Christ in you — the living Lord himself, by his Spirit, taking up residence within his people (Gal. 2:20, “Christ lives in me”; Rom. 8:9–10). The whole Christ, present, indwelling, now — in the humblest Gentile believer in Colossae, in Old Joe. And this indwelling is “the hope of glory.” “Hope” here is not a wistful maybe; it is settled certainty. Because Christ is in you now, the glory to come is sure: “when Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:4). The present indwelling is the pledge and down payment of the coming splendour — God’s own deposit, guaranteeing that the story ends in glory. This is the answer to the whole letter’s error: you do not need a mediator to reach a distant God, for God in Christ already lives within you, and that is your unbreakable hope. cf. Rom. 8:30; 2 Cor. 1:22.

For Old Joe — what does this dense verse actually mean? Strip it to the bone and it says this: the greatest treasure God ever kept hidden turns out to be Jesus himself, come to live inside ordinary people like Old Joe — and having him within is the cast-iron guarantee that glory is coming. Picture it this way. Imagine the King of all the earth choosing to leave his palace and move, in person, into a labourer’s little cottage — not to visit, but to live there, under that humble roof, day and night. The neighbours would shake their heads in wonder: why there, of all places? But here is the thing that makes the heart race — if the King himself has taken up residence in your cottage now, then it is utterly certain that one day he means to bring you home to his palace. He has not moved in to leave you in the cottage forever. “Christ in you” is the King in the cottage; “the hope of glory” is the palace that must surely follow. Old Joe does not have to climb to God, or earn his way up, or feel worthy enough. The King has already moved in — and that settles where Old Joe will spend forever.

verseByVerse.quote: Him we proclaim, warning everyone and teaching everyone with all wisdom, that we may present everyone mature in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Him we proclaim” — a Person, not a programme. In the Greek the very first word is emphatic: Him. Not “it” — not a set of rules, not a code of conduct, not a new religious system, not a ladder of disciplines to climb. Him. The whole burden of Christian preaching is a Person: Christ himself, to be known, trusted, and loved. This lands like a hammer on the Colossian error, which was busy peddling exactly the opposite — regulations, festivals, food laws, angel-rituals, secret know-how (the religious machinery of ch. 2). Paul will not preach a machine; he heralds a Master. “We proclaim” (katangellomen) is the word for a public herald’s open announcement, not the whispered initiation of a secret society. And here is the heart of it for Old Joe: Christianity is not first a list of things to do; it is first a Person to have. The rules are not the gospel; Christ is. You do not get Christ by keeping the rules — you get the rules kept by having Christ. cf. 1 Cor. 1:23; 2 Cor. 4:5.

“Warning everyone” — warning about what? True ministry has a warning side, not only a comforting one. The word (nouthetountes) means to admonish, to put someone in mind of danger, to counsel them out of harm’s way — the very thing Paul did at Ephesus “night and day…with tears” (Acts 20:31). Warning about what? About everything that threatens the soul: chiefly, here, the lure away from the all-sufficient Christ onto the empty promises of the false teachers (the danger that fills ch. 2); and behind that, the deceitfulness of sin, the peril of drifting, the seriousness of one day standing before God. To warn is not the opposite of love; it is love — the shepherd who never tells the sheep about the cliff or the wolf is not kind, he is faithless. A father shouts a warning to the child wandering into the road precisely because he loves him. A ministry that only soothes and never warns has stopped caring for people’s real danger. cf. Acts 20:31; Ezek. 33:7–9.

“Teaching everyone with all wisdom” — what does Paul mean? If warning turns people away from danger, teaching builds them up in the truth — the two go together, the negative and the positive of one ministry. And it is done “with all wisdom.” Not the world’s cleverness, and certainly not the counterfeit “wisdom” the false teachers boasted (which has only “an appearance of wisdom,” 2:23), but the true wisdom found in Christ himself, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (2:3). “All wisdom” carries two notes: the full counsel of God, holding nothing back; and the skill to apply it rightly — for teaching is not dumping facts on people, but wisely fitting God’s truth to each real life so that it actually takes root and grows. And mark the drumbeat of this verse: everyone…everyone…everyone — three times. Against a heresy that hoarded its secrets for an inner ring, Paul’s warning and teaching are for every single believer: no elite, no inner circle, no second tier.

“That we may present everyone mature in Christ” — the goal of it all. Here is the aim that drives every sermon, every warning, every patient hour of teaching. “Present” (parastēsōmen) is the same word Paul used in v. 22 — the presentation of God’s people before him, the great Day in view — and the whole labour of ministry now bends toward that day. The goal is that everyone be “mature in Christ.” The word (teleios) means complete, full-grown, brought to the intended end — not a flawless saint but a grown-up one. Let Old Joe be clear on what this is not. It is not sinless perfection — he will not be without fault or struggle this side of glory, and maturity is not the day his sin finally vanishes. It is not head-knowledge — a man can know the whole Bible and still be a spiritual toddler. It is not religious performance — keeping rules, ticking boxes, looking the part. And it is not a higher tier for an elite few (the very thing the false teachers dangled); it is the ordinary goal for every believer. What it is: growing up into Christ — rooted, steady, discerning, Christlike in character, no longer blown about by every new teaching, able to stand on his own feet and feed himself from God’s Word. Think of a child becoming a full-grown adult: no one expects a newborn to be faultless, but everyone expects a baby to grow. A sapling and a great oak share the very same life — the oak is simply that life grown to its fullness. That is maturity: not a different Christianity from the new convert’s, but the same Christ-life grown up, sturdy, and bearing fruit. And it is fixed “in Christ” — for to grow up is simply to become more and more like him. cf. Eph. 4:13–15; Heb. 5:13–14.

verseByVerse.quote: For this I toil, struggling with all his energy that he powerfully works within me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I toil” — Paul turns to himself. Notice the shift. A moment ago it was “we proclaim” (v. 28), the shared work of Paul and his fellow-labourers. Now it narrows to a single man: “I toil.” Paul has just laid out the goal of all ministry; now he lets the Colossians see what it costs him personally to pursue it. And remember where he sits as he writes — in a prison cell (4:18). He is no armchair theorist describing labour from a safe distance; he is a man pouring out his very life, in chains, for churches he has never even met (2:1). The vision of presenting people mature in Christ is no tidy slogan to him; it is the thing he sweats and bleeds for.

“For this” — for what? “For this I toil” — that is, for the goal just named in v. 28: to present everyone mature in Christ. Every ounce of Paul’s labour is aimed at that one target. He does not toil for fame, or money, or comfort, or a quiet retirement; he does not even toil merely to win converts and then leave them as babes. He spends himself for one thing — that the people of God grow up complete in Christ. The goal governs the labour. A ministry that forgets “mature in Christ” has forgotten why it should toil at all.

“I toil, struggling” — the Christian life and ministry are hard work. Paul reaches for two strenuous words. “Toil” (kopiō) means to labour until you are bone-weary, the sweat-soaked work of a field-hand at harvest. “Struggling” (agōnizomenos) is the word of the athlete straining every sinew in the contest — it is where we get our “agonize.” This is worth saying plainly, because some imagine the Christian life is meant to be a gentle, effortless drift. It is not. Following Christ, fighting sin, serving his people, holding fast under pressure — all of it calls for real, costly, wearying effort. Paul does not coast; he agonizes. There is no growing up into Christ, for the apostle or for Old Joe, without sweat.

And yet — it is God who supplies the strength. Look how the sentence ends: “struggling with all his energy that he powerfully works within me.” Paul strains every muscle, but the power he strains with is not his own — it is God’s might, energizing him from the inside. (Paul even plays on the word: God energizes the very energy Paul labours by.) Here is the great balance the whole Bible keeps, nowhere more clearly than in a verse this one echoes: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:12–13). Maximum effort and total dependence, held together in one breath — not fifty-fifty, but fully Paul’s striving and fully God’s working.

Old Joe can tumble into either of two ditches here. The first is “let go and let God” — the notion that he should simply relax, surrender, and wait for God to do everything, since any effort of his own is mere “flesh.” But Paul did not let go; he toiled to the point of agony, and Scripture never treats hard work as unspiritual. This ditch breeds passivity, spiritual laziness, and a stalled, fruitless faith — and then blames God for the barrenness our own sloth produced. The second ditch is the opposite: “it is all up to me” — gritting the teeth and trying to white-knuckle the Christian life on sheer willpower. This breeds pride when it seems to be working, and despair and burnout when it is not; at bottom it is simply self-reliance wearing religious clothes. The truth runs right between them: work hard, and lean hard. Strive with everything you have — and draw every ounce of the strength from God, moment by moment. The harder Paul worked, the more utterly he depended on the strength of Another; effort and dependence were never rivals but partners.

Picture a sailing boat. The crew must do real, sweating work — hoist the sails, trim the lines, lean into the ropes; a lazy crew goes nowhere. And yet not one inch of progress comes from their muscle alone — it is the wind that drives the boat home. No wind, and all their heaving is useless; but the wind fills only the sails that hands have laboured to set. So it is with Old Joe. He is not to sit in the harbour waiting for God to move the boat without him (that is the first ditch); nor is he to row himself to exhaustion as though there were no wind at all (that is the second). He is to set the sails — pray, fight sin, feed on the Word, serve the church, keep going — and let the wind of God’s own power carry him on. The sweat is real, and it is his; the strength is real, and it is God’s. cf. Phil. 2:12–13; 1 Cor. 15:10 (“I worked harder than any of them — though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me”).

2.title: Fullness in Christ: Warnings Against Every Supplement
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is the letter’s most polemical section and its most theologically precise: the fullness that is in Christ alone (vv. 9–10) is set directly against every system that claims to supplement him. The chapter moves through three interlocking arguments. First (vv. 1–7): be rooted in Christ, built up in him, established in him — the metaphors of depth, growth, and stability describe the Christian who has genuinely understood what they have in him. Second (vv. 8–15): the Colossian philosophy is empty deceit; in Christ you have been circumcised with a true circumcision, buried and raised with him, forgiven all your trespasses, the law’s record of debt against you cancelled and nailed to the cross. Third (vv. 16–23): therefore let no one disqualify you by judging you on food, drink, festivals, new moons, or sabbaths — these are shadows; the substance is Christ. And the self-made religion that looks impressive is actually of no value against the indulgence of the flesh.

The theological heart of the chapter is verse 9–10: “in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him.” The fullness is Christ’s ongoing reality; the filling is the Colossians’ already-accomplished fact. Their fullness is given, settled, possessed. The false teachers are offering what the Colossians already have.

The legal image of verse 14 — “cancelling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands” — is one of the most vivid pictures of forgiveness in the New Testament. The image is of a written document of indebtedness, a bond or IOU, that records what is owed. God takes this document — the record of every sin, every violation, every debt we owe him — and nails it to the cross. The debt is not merely forgiven; the document is destroyed, posted publicly at the site of Christ’s execution, so that all can see: this debt has been paid in full, publicly, finally, at the cross.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Rooted and Built Up in Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul opens the chapter with an expression of pastoral anguish that intensifies the chapter’s warning: he is “struggling” for the Colossians and the Laodiceans — people who have never seen his face — that their hearts would be encouraged and knit together in love, with the full assurance of understanding and the knowledge of God’s mystery, which is Christ. The goal of his struggle is their encouragement, their unity, and their certainty; and the content of that certainty is Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

The warning is introduced gently: “I say this in order that no one may delude you with plausible-sounding arguments.” The false teaching was not obviously wrong; it was plausible. It sounded like wisdom. It offered something real-seeming: fuller knowledge, more complete access to God, a more sophisticated understanding of the spiritual world. The antidote is not suspicion of all philosophy but deep rootedness in Christ — the one in whom all wisdom and knowledge are hidden, not in any competing system.
verseByVerse.theology:
All the Treasures of Wisdom Hidden in Christ

Colossians 2:3 — “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” — is the epistemological foundation of the Reformed tradition’s approach to all knowledge. Cornelius Van Til’s presuppositionalism, Abraham Kuyper’s sphere sovereignty, Francis Schaeffer’s integrated Christian worldview: all are ultimately grounded in this text. All genuine wisdom and knowledge find their coherence and source in Christ. This does not mean that only Christians can know things; it means that all knowledge that is genuinely true is “thinking God’s thoughts after him,” participating (knowingly or not) in the structure of reality that Christ created and sustains. The Christian intellectual task is to follow wisdom wherever it leads, knowing that it leads ultimately to the one in whom all wisdom is hidden.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian philosophy offered esoteric wisdom that seemed to go beyond what the gospel provided. Paul says: all the wisdom you are seeking is already hidden in Christ. You are not lacking wisdom; you have not been exploring deeply enough the one in whom wisdom dwells. Now: The Christian who turns to secular philosophy, psychology, or spirituality for the wisdom that Christ supposedly cannot provide has accepted the false teachers’ premise. All genuine wisdom, wherever it is found, is a trace of the one in whom all wisdom is hidden. The Christian engages with every source of wisdom while recognizing that Christ is its ultimate source and criterion.

verseByVerse.quote: For I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you and for those at Laodicea and for all who have not seen me face to face,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you” — here is the heart of a true pastor. Paul lets the Colossians look straight into his inner life, and what they see is a man labouring for them — not for what he can get from them, but for their good. Then comes the astonishing detail: he struggles “for you and for those at Laodicea and for all who have not seen me face to face.” Paul had never been to Colossae. He did not plant the church — Epaphras did (1:7). He had never met these people, never seen their faces, would not have known them in the street. And yet he agonizes for them. That is the mark of a shepherd after Christ’s own heart: his care is not rationed out only to his friends, his own converts, or those who can repay him — it reaches to sheep in a valley he has never even visited, simply because they belong to Christ. A hireling cares only for what the flock does for him; the true shepherd cares for the flock itself (cf. John 10:12–13). Paul loved people he had never laid eyes on, because he loved their Lord.

“How great a struggle” — and it cost him dearly. The word is agōn (we get our “agony” from it) — the all-out exertion of the wrestler or the runner in the contest. It is the very word he has just used of his ministry in 1:29 (“struggling with all his energy”); now that toil narrows from “everyone” down to these believers by name. And notice his circumstances: he writes in chains (4:18), far away, unable to visit them, to preach to them, to sit at their side. So how does a caged apostle “struggle” for a church he cannot reach? Chiefly on his knees. His agony is the unseen labour of intercession — wrestling prayer, sleepless concern, the daily pouring out of his heart to God on their behalf — exactly the way Epaphras was “always struggling on your behalf in his prayers” (4:12, the same word). Pastoral love is not a warm feeling at a distance; it is hard, costly, hidden work. And it is not aimless: Paul struggles toward a goal — the goal he sets out in the very next verse, that their hearts be encouraged, knit together in love, and brought to the full assurance of knowing Christ. He wrestles in prayer so that they will stand.

There is quiet comfort here for Old Joe, and a quiet summons. The comfort: somewhere, perhaps, an unseen saint is wrestling in prayer for him by name, as Paul did for strangers and Epaphras did for friends — the church is held up by hidden hands folded in prayer. And the summons: this is what love looks like. To care for another’s soul — even the soul of someone we have never met — enough to labour for it before God is to love as Paul loved, and as Christ loves still. cf. Rom. 15:30; 2 Cor. 11:28.

verseByVerse.quote: that their hearts may be encouraged, being knit together in love, to reach all the riches of full assurance of understanding and the knowledge of God’s mystery, which is Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Knit together in love” — the unity Paul seeks is not organizational uniformity but the organic binding-together of a community by love, the love that is poured into hearts by the Spirit (Rom 5:5). “All the riches of full assurance” — Paul desires not tentative, anxious, uncertain faith but the confident, assured faith of those who know what they have in Christ. The assurance is grounded not in subjective experience but in the objective reality: Christ, in whom all wisdom is hidden.

verseByVerse.quote: I say this in order that no one may delude you with plausible-sounding arguments. For though I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing to see your good order and the firmness of your faith in Christ. Therefore, as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him, rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, just as you were taught, abounding in thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Plausible-sounding arguments” (pithanologia) — the word suggests rhetoric that persuades not by truth but by the appearance of truth, clever and convincing but hollow at its core. Paul warns against it not by providing a counter-argument for every false claim but by pointing to the alternative: rootedness in Christ. The metaphor of “rooted and built up” combines the agricultural (roots going deep into soil) and the architectural (being built up on a foundation). Both images speak of stability, of depth, of the capacity to withstand pressure that shallower or less well-founded structures cannot. “Abounding in thanksgiving” — the grateful heart is the heart that knows what it has; ingratitude opens the door to the false teacher’s offer of something more.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The warning is now direct: “See to it that no one takes you captive by philosophy and empty deceit.” The false teachers’ system is exposed: it is according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ. The contrast with Christ is then developed with explosive theological force: the whole fullness of deity dwells in him bodily; you have been filled in him; in him you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands; you were buried with him, raised with him, made alive with him; your trespasses were forgiven; the record of your debt was cancelled and nailed to the cross; the rulers and authorities were disarmed and put to open shame in him.

The cascade of completed actions — you have been filled, you were circumcised, you were buried, you were raised, you were made alive, your trespasses were forgiven, the debt was cancelled, the rulers were disarmed — is an overwhelming statement of what has already happened to the believer in Christ. Everything the false teachers are offering as a supplement, the Colossians already possess. Their baptism (vv. 12–13) was the public enactment of what Christ accomplished: burial with him into death, raising with him into life. Nothing more is needed, because nothing less than everything has been given.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cancellation of the Debt and the Disarming of the Powers

Colossians 2:13–15 contains two of the most vivid metaphors for the atonement in the New Testament. First, the legal metaphor: the “record of debt” (cheirographon) that stood against us — the written bond of indebtedness, the document that recorded every sin and violation — has been cancelled, taken out of the way, nailed to the cross. The debt is not merely forgiven; the document is destroyed. Second, the military metaphor: the rulers and authorities who held humanity in their power through guilt and the law’s accusation have been “disarmed” and put to open shame — led in a triumphal procession like conquered enemies behind the victorious general. These two images together show what the cross accomplished: liberation from guilt (the debt cancelled) and liberation from spiritual bondage (the powers defeated).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian philosophy appealed to the elemental spirits and cosmic powers as real and threatening forces that needed to be placated through ritual observance. Paul says: those powers have been disarmed. They are defeated enemies, paraded in public shame behind the triumphing Christ. You do not placate them; you stand on the victory that has already been won. Now: The Christian who lives in fear of spiritual powers — who approaches life with anxiety about demonic influence, spiritual attack, or cosmic forces working against them — needs to hear this: the powers have been disarmed. Christ has triumphed. The fear of powers that have been publicly defeated is not piety; it is a failure to reckon with the victory of the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: See to it that no one takes you captive by philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ. For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him, who is the head of all rule and authority.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Takes you captive” (sylagōgōn) — the image is of a kidnapper or a soldier carrying off prisoners of war. The false teaching is not a gentle invitation to greater spirituality; it is an act of capture, a taking into bondage. “According to the elemental spirits of the world” (stoicheia tou kosmou) — the basic ordering principles and powers of the old age, the forces that govern life outside of Christ. Whatever the Colossian teachers meant by these, Paul’s point is the same: they are not of Christ, and therefore they have no claim on those who are in Christ. “The whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” — pan to plērōma tēs theotētos sōmatikōs: every attribute, every perfection, every power of God is present in Christ, not distributed among a spiritual hierarchy, not accessible only through additional rituals, but fully available in the one who became flesh and died and rose. And: “you have been filled in him” — the perfect passive of plēróō: this is your present, completed condition.

verseByVerse.quote: In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God, who raised him from the dead… And you, who were dead in your trespasses… God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses, by canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross. He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The true circumcision is the circumcision of Christ — not a physical act performed on the flesh but the spiritual act of putting off the entire “body of the flesh,” the old nature in its totality. This is what baptism enacted and what faith received: death and resurrection with Christ. “The powerful working of God who raised him from the dead” — the same power that raised Jesus from the grave is the power at work in every conversion and every act of sanctification.

The cheirographon — the certificate of debt: Paul’s image in v. 14 is one of the most electrifying in all of his letters, but it requires explanation. The Greek cheirographon (literally “hand-written document”) was a technical commercial and legal term in the ancient world for a promissory note or certificate of debt — a document handwritten by the debtor, acknowledging what was owed and signed as a binding commitment. In Greco-Roman legal practice such documents were kept until the debt was paid, then cancelled by “wiping out” the ink (the Greek exaleiphō, v. 14, means literally “to wipe out, to erase” — the method of cancelling ink on a papyrus document by washing it off) or by crossing through it. Paul’s interpretation: the record of our moral obligations to God, the accumulated certificate of everything we owe and have failed to pay — every commandment violated, every debt of obedience unpaid — was a cheirographon standing against us. God did not merely file it away or suppress it. He “set it aside, nailing it to the cross.”

Nailed to the cross: Roman soldiers routinely attached the written charge sheet (titulus) to the cross above the crucified criminal — the placard above Jesus read “King of the Jews” (John 19:19–22). Paul may be deliberately invoking this image: our debt-document was the placard nailed to the cross. The document that recorded what we owed was absorbed into the body of Christ, cancelled by his death. The debt is not outstanding; the record is not merely forgiven — it has been nailed to the wood and the death of Christ has satisfied what it demanded. The rulers and authorities — whatever spiritual powers the Colossian teachers feared — are now like conquered kings displayed in a Roman triumph, their weapons taken, their dignity stripped, marched behind the victorious Christ for all to see that the victory is complete.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The practical applications of the theological victory are now drawn: if the powers are disarmed, if the debt is cancelled, if you are complete in Christ — then let no one judge you in matters of food, drink, festivals, new moons, or sabbaths. These were the specific demands of the Colossian philosophy. Paul’s response is not to debate the merits of each requirement but to reframe them all: they are “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.” The shadow is real — it tells you something about the substance that casts it — but once the substance has arrived, the shadow has served its purpose. To return to the shadow when the substance is present is not greater piety; it is a failure of perception.

The warning against “self-made religion” (v. 23) — ethelothrēskia, voluntary or self-chosen worship — is one of the sharpest critiques of false spirituality in the New Testament. It looks impressive: asceticism, severity to the body, false humility. But it has “no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh.” The very thing the ascetic program claims to address — the sinful desires of the body — is the thing it cannot actually defeat. Only death and resurrection with Christ — the reality described in verses 11–15 — accomplishes what self-discipline merely manages, and poorly.
verseByVerse.theology:
Shadow and Substance: The Old Covenant as Anticipation

Paul’s description of the Mosaic observances as “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (v. 17) is the hermeneutical principle underlying all Reformed typological interpretation of the Old Testament. The ceremonial law — the festivals, the sabbaths, the food laws, the sacrificial system — was genuinely given by God and genuinely pointed forward to the reality that was coming. But it was always a shadow, not the substance; always anticipation, not fulfilment. The substance arrived in Christ. To return to the shadow when the substance is present is not faithfulness to the law; it is a failure to read what the law was always saying.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian teachers were using Jewish observances as part of their syncretic system, insisting that the Colossians needed to keep certain days and food laws and festivals. Paul says: these were shadows pointing to Christ; Christ has come. Now: The same principle applies to any Christian movement that makes Old Testament ceremonial practices the standard of Christian spirituality. The principles of justice, love, and holiness that the ceremonial law expressed are fulfilled in Christ and applied by the Spirit. The specific ceremonies have been fulfilled in him who was their substance all along.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath. These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ. Let no one disqualify you, insisting on asceticism and worship of angels, going on in detail about visions, puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind, and not holding fast to the Head, from whom the whole body, nourished and knit together through its joints and ligaments, grows with a growth that is from God.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Let no one pass judgment on you” — the freedom of the Christian is real and must be defended. The freedom to eat, to observe or not observe certain days, to refuse the demands of systems that claim to add to Christ — this freedom must be maintained, not surrendered to social or religious pressure. “Worship of angels” and “going on in detail about visions” suggest the visionary and mystical elements of the Colossian heresy: a form of spirituality that prided itself on supernatural experiences and angelic mediation. Paul’s diagnosis is devastating: “puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind.” The impressive spiritual display is actually a form of self-inflation, rooted not in genuine encounter with God but in the flesh’s desire for status and recognition. “Not holding fast to the Head” — this is the fundamental problem: the false teacher has lost connection to Christ, the head from whom all true nourishment and growth come.

verseByVerse.quote: If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the world, why, as if you were still alive in the world, do you submit to regulations — ‘Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch’…? These have indeed an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits” — the death-with-Christ described in verse 12 means that the Colossians have already died to the elemental spirits and their demands. To submit to those demands again is to act as though the death never happened, as though they are still “alive in the world” in the old sense. The regulations — “do not handle, do not taste, do not touch” — are not morally wrong in themselves; they are spiritually useless as a means of addressing the flesh’s indulgence. The flesh is not conquered by external prohibition; it is conquered by death and resurrection with Christ.

Ethelothrēskia — self-imposed religion (v. 23, ESV “self-made religion”): Paul coins a word — ethelothrēskia — that appears nowhere else in the entire Greek language before or after this verse. It combines ethelō (to will, to choose) with thrēskeia (religion, worship): “will-worship,” “self-directed religious practice,” worship chosen by the human will rather than commanded by divine revelation. It is the technical term for religion that originates in human religious creativity rather than in God’s self-revelation. The false teachers’ system was impressive in its ascetic severity and its claim to spiritual depth — it had “an appearance of wisdom.” Paul’s one-word verdict: it is self-will dressed up as devotion. The most dangerous religion is always the one that looks most like real piety while being rooted in human initiative rather than divine grace. “Of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh” — asceticism’s failure: the flesh is not mortified by dietary restrictions. It relocates — from gluttony to pride in one’s own spiritual discipline. The ascetic who refuses certain foods to discipline his flesh discovers that the flesh is merely redirected to pride in its own discipline. Self-made religion is the most dangerous religion because it has just enough appearance of wisdom to be mistaken for the real thing.

3.title: Set Your Minds on Things Above: The Old and the New
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is the ethical consequence of everything chapters 1–2 have established. The logic is characteristically Pauline: because of who you are in Christ (indicative), live accordingly (imperative). You have died with Christ; you have been raised with Christ; your life is hidden with Christ in God; Christ is your life. Therefore: set your minds on things above, put to death what is earthly in you, put off the old self, put on the new self — and let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, the word of Christ dwell in you richly, and everything you do be done in the name of the Lord Jesus.

The chapter’s structure is the structure of the gospel applied to daily life: the negative movement of putting off (vv. 5–11), and the positive movement of putting on (vv. 12–17). The things to be put off are the practices of the old self — sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, covetousness, anger, wrath, malice, slander, obscene talk, lying. The things to be put on are the character of the new self — compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, patience, forbearing one another, forgiving each other, and above all, love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony.

The chapter then extends this transformation into the household (vv. 18–4:1): the practical ordering of the most intimate human relationships — wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters — under the lordship of Christ. These are not arbitrary social regulations; they are the gospel working its way into the fabric of daily life, the supremacy of Christ (chapter 1) arriving at the breakfast table, the bedroom, and the workplace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Set Your Minds on Things Above
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter opens with two of the most important words in Colossians: “If then you have been raised with Christ” — but the “if” is not an uncertainty; in Greek it assumes a true condition: “since you have been raised with Christ.” The resurrection with Christ is the Colossians’ established condition, the accomplished reality on which everything else rests. From this foundation, the imperative follows: seek the things that are above; set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth.

This is not escapism or world-denial; it is the reorientation of the entire life around the reality of Christ’s lordship, which is “above” in the sense of being ultimate, final, and true. The “things above” are not the celestial geography of the false teachers’ angelic hierarchy; they are the things that are real in the deepest sense because they are rooted in Christ who sits at God’s right hand. And the statement of verse 3 — “your life is hidden with Christ in God” — is one of the most consoling in the letter: hidden, secure, inviolable, located in the safest place in the universe.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Hidden Life and the Security of the Believer in Christ

Colossians 3:3 — “your life is hidden with Christ in God” — is one of the New Testament’s most comprehensive statements of the security of the believer. The life of the Christian is not exposed to the attacks of the world, the flesh, or the devil in any ultimate sense; it is hidden, concealed, kept safe in the most secure location possible: with Christ, in God. Reformed theology has always grounded assurance of salvation not in the believer’s performance but in the security of their position: in Christ, kept by God. This is why the Christian can face the world’s hostility and the flesh’s internal rebellion without ultimate despair; the life that matters is in a place nothing can reach.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were being told that their spiritual security depended on correct navigation of the angelic hierarchy, proper observance of festivals and food laws, and achievement of special spiritual states. Paul says: your life is hidden with Christ in God. There is no spiritual power that can reach it; no ritual failure that can revoke it; no ignorance of esoteric knowledge that can diminish it. Now: The Christian whose sense of security rises and falls with their spiritual performance — who feels secure on days of devotional discipline and insecure on days of failure — needs to hear this: your life is hidden. It is not at risk. It is kept by the one whose power infinitely exceeds every force that would threaten it.

verseByVerse.quote: If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Seek” and “set your minds” (zēteite and phroneite) — two present imperatives, indicating continuous, ongoing activity. This is not a one-time reorientation but the sustained direction of desire and thought toward Christ. “Where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God” — the exalted Christ of the hymn (1:18–19) is also the Christ of your daily seeking. The things above are not abstract ideals but the concrete reality of Christ’s present lordship, already established, already operative. “When Christ who is your life appears” — the eschatological horizon of the entire ethical section: Christ’s return is the moment when the hidden life becomes visible, when what is true in Christ will be publicly, universally manifest. The Christian life is lived in the time between the hiddenness and the appearing, in confident hope of the glory that the appearing will reveal.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–11 — Put to Death, Put Off
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The imperative of putting to death what is earthly follows directly from the indicative of having died with Christ.
