Because you have died (3:3), therefore put to death what belongs to your earthly nature (3:5). The logic is not “try harder” but “reckon what is true.” The death with Christ was real; the ongoing mortification of the flesh is the daily application of that real death to specific desires, habits, and patterns of behaviour.

The list of what must be put to death (vv. 5–9) moves from individual sins (sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, covetousness) to relational sins (anger, wrath, malice, slander, obscene talk, lying). The reason given is profound: “you have put off the old self with its practices and have put on the new self.” The change of clothing has already happened; the ongoing putting off is the appropriation of that change into daily life. And the new self is continually “being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator” (v. 10) — the process of sanctification as the progressive restoration of the image of God in the believer.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mortification: Putting to Death What Christ Has Already Condemned

John Owen’s great treatise On the Mortification of Sin is the most sustained Reformed treatment of what Paul commands in Colossians 3:5. Owen’s central principle — “be killing sin, or it will be killing you” — reflects Paul’s logic exactly. The mortification Paul calls for is not the ascetic self-punishment that the Colossian false teachers practiced and Paul has just condemned (2:23); it is the Spirit-enabled application of the cross to specific sinful desires, the practical reckoning with what Christ accomplished: these desires belong to the old self that died in Christ; by the Spirit I put them to death.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were being offered an ascetic program that promised to deal with the flesh by external denial. Paul says: that program has no value in stopping the flesh’s indulgence (2:23). The real program is mortification — not external prohibition but the internal death-dealing of the Spirit to specific desires. The difference is not severity (asceticism can be more severe than mortification) but source: mortification flows from union with the crucified Christ. Now: The Christian who is fighting sin through willpower and self-discipline alone is using the wrong weapons. Mortification is spiritual warfare: the application of Christ’s death to specific sin patterns, in prayer, by the Spirit, in the community of faith. The fight is real; the weapon is the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry. On account of these the wrath of God is coming. In these you too once walked, when you were living in them. But now you must put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth. Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old self with its practices.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Put to death therefore what is earthly in you” — the word is violent: kill, execute, put to death. This is not a gentle suggestion to reduce sinful tendencies but a command to execute them. The word “therefore” connects back to the indicative: because you have died with Christ, put to death what belongs to the old nature. “Covetousness, which is idolatry” — the insight that connects economic desire to false worship: whatever you desire more than God is your functional god. Covetousness is not merely wanting too many things; it is the displacement of God from the centre of desire by created goods. The relational sins of verses 8–9 — anger, wrath, malice, slander, obscene talk, lying — are the social consequences of the internal sins of verses 5–7: the disordered heart produces disordered relationships. “You have put off the old self” — already accomplished in Christ. The imperative of verse 9 is the ongoing appropriation of the accomplished reality.

verseByVerse.quote: and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator. Here there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator” — the ongoing process of sanctification understood as the progressive restoration of the imago Dei. The image in which humanity was originally made (Gen 1:26–27) was marred by the fall; in Christ, the new humanity, the image-restoration has begun and is in continuous progress. The knowledge in which it is renewed is the knowledge of God — the practical, relational knowledge of the one who made us, which produces conformity to his character. “Christ is all, and in all” — the climax of the ethical section and the summary of the entire letter: every human distinction dissolves in the community of the new self, because the only category that ultimately matters is whether one is in Christ, and Christ is all in all.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having commanded the putting off of the old self, Paul now commands the putting on of the new: the character of those who are “God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved.” The virtues of the new self — compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, patience, forbearance, forgiveness — are not a personal achievement program but the shape of the character that the Spirit produces in those who are genuinely united with Christ and genuinely putting to death the old self.

The governing virtue, above all the others, is love: “which binds everything together in perfect harmony.” Love is not one virtue among others but the one that gives all the others their form and energy. And ruling over the whole is the peace of Christ, for which the community was “called in the one body.” The word of Christ is to dwell in them richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs with thankfulness. The community that puts on the new self is a singing, thankful, Word-saturated, peace-ruled community.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Virtues of the New Self as the Character of Christ

The list of virtues in Colossians 3:12–15 is nothing less than a portrait of Christ himself: compassionate, kind, humble, meek, patient, forgiving, loving, peaceful. Reformed theology understands sanctification as progressive conformity to the image of Christ (Rom 8:29); the virtues Paul commands here are the specific contours of that image. They are not generated by the believer through moral effort; they are produced by the Spirit as the fruit of genuine union with Christ (compare the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22–23). The community that puts on these virtues is the community that is becoming what it already is in Christ: holy and beloved.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian community, like every early Christian community, was a mixture of people from very different backgrounds — Jewish, Greek, slave, free — with very different habits of relating and conflicting. The virtues Paul commands were counter-cultural in every direction: humility was scorned by Graeco-Roman aristocratic culture; forgiveness was a novelty in a world organized around honour and revenge. Now: The church remains the most diverse social reality in the world, and the virtues Paul commands remain equally counter-cultural. The church that is genuinely putting on compassion, kindness, humility, and forbearance will look radically different from any other community the world contains, because these virtues are the character of the one who was raised for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Put on then, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience, bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive. And above all these put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony.
verseByVerse.commentary: “God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved” — three descriptions of identity that precede every imperative. The virtues are to be put on not to become God’s chosen but because you are already his chosen. The identity is prior to the ethics; the ethics flow from the identity. “Bearing with one another” and “forgiving each other” — the two relational practices most needed in a community under pressure: endurance of one another’s irritating qualities, and the forgiveness that refuses to let grievances harden into alienation. “As the Lord has forgiven you” — the ground and measure of Christian forgiveness: not “as you deserve” or “as you have apologized” but as the Lord forgave — freely, fully, prior to merit, at great cost. “Love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony” — the syndesmos tēs teleiotētos, the bond of completeness: the ligament that holds the whole body together in the maturity for which Paul has been praying.

verseByVerse.quote: And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in one body. And be thankful. Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, with thankfulness in your hearts to God. And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.
verseByVerse.commentary: “The peace of Christ rule in your hearts” — brabeuetō, let it act as umpire or referee, making the final call in situations of conflict and uncertainty. When decisions must be made, when relationships are in tension, when the community is pulled in different directions — let the peace of Christ be the deciding factor. “The word of Christ dwell in you richly” — not merely to be consulted occasionally but to take up permanent, spacious residence: enolkeitō plousios, inhabit you in abundance. The Word-saturated community teaches and admonishes one another; its mutual ministry of the Word is the mechanism by which the word dwells richly in the whole. “Whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus” — the most comprehensive statement of the lordship of Christ over daily life in the New Testament. Nothing falls outside it: not eating or drinking (1 Cor 10:31), not family relationships, not work, not rest. Everything, in his name.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The household code that closes the ethical section applies the lordship of Christ to the most intimate sphere of daily life: the household. In the ancient world, the household was the basic unit of society — the structure within which most of life was lived, economic activity organized, and social relationships defined. Paul does not abolish the household structure but transforms it: every relationship within the household is to be conducted “as is fitting in the Lord,” or “fearing the Lord,” or “as to the Lord and not to men.” The lordship of Christ is the governing reality of the breakfast table, the workplace, and the master-slave relationship.

The household code is one of Paul’s most contested passages, particularly the instructions about wives and slaves. Three things must be held together: first, Paul is working within the existing social structures of his time rather than abolishing them by direct command; second, the reciprocity he builds in (husbands love, fathers do not embitter, masters treat justly) was genuinely counter-cultural in a world where the authority of husband, father, and master was absolute; third, the principles he applies — love, justice, what is right and fair — contain within them the seeds of the social transformation that has over time dismantled the worst features of those structures.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lordship of Christ in the Household: Sacred and Ordinary

The household code illustrates one of Reformed theology’s most important convictions: there is no sacred-secular divide. The lordship of Christ claimed in the great hymn of chapter 1 arrives in chapter 3 at the level of household management, parenting, and the workplace. Abraham Kuyper’s “every square inch” is not abstract theology; it is the practical implication of “whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus” (3:17). The Christian who is an excellent spouse, a patient parent, and an honest worker is doing theology in the most concrete possible form.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Graeco-Roman household was organized around the absolute authority of the paterfamilias — husband, father, master. His authority was legally absolute. Paul does not abolish this structure but fills it with a different spirit: love, not domination; encouragement, not provocation; justice, not exploitation. The counterpart to every command of submission is a command of love and care that was genuinely counter-cultural. Now: The application of these principles in contemporary household and work relationships continues to produce the same counter-cultural witness: the Christian employee who works with integrity “as to the Lord” even when unsupervised; the Christian employer who treats workers with justice and fairness; the Christian parent who encourages rather than exasperates. Each is a small enactment of the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord. Husbands, love your wives, and do not be harsh with them. Children, obey your parents in everything, for this pleases the Lord. Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged.
verseByVerse.commentary: Each pair of instructions has a command and a motivation. The wife’s submission is “fitting in the Lord” — the standard is not cultural convention but the ordering of the new community under Christ’s lordship. The husband’s love is the radical counterpart: not merely affection but the kind of self-giving love that Ephesians 5:25 defines as the love of Christ for the church, willing his wife’s good above his own comfort. “Do not be harsh with them” — the counter-cultural word to the husband who possessed by law an authority that could easily curdle into domination. “Lest they become discouraged” — Paul’s concern for children is their flourishing, not merely their compliance. The discouraged child is evidence of a father who has used his authority as power rather than as stewardship.

verseByVerse.quote: Bondservants, obey in everything those who are your earthly masters, not by way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord. Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. You are serving the Lord Christ… Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men” — the transformation of work: not for the approval of the human master but for the Lord whose approval is the only ultimate one. The slave who works with integrity when the master is watching and with equal integrity when he is not has understood the lordship of Christ over all of life. “You will receive the inheritance as your reward” — an extraordinary promise to slaves who, by definition, could inherit nothing under Roman law: from the Lord who is no respecter of legal status, the slave who serves faithfully will receive the inheritance of the sons. “Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly” — the masters too have a Master in heaven who will hold them accountable. The hierarchical structure is not abolished, but it is placed under the judgment of the one before whom all hierarchies are levelled.

4.title: Devoted to Prayer: Wisdom, Words, and the Gospel Network
4.overview:
The final chapter of Colossians is shorter and more personal than the preceding chapters but carries the letter’s theology into two final areas: the Christian’s relationship to prayer and to the world (vv. 2–6), and the network of relationships through which the gospel advances (vv. 7–18). Together they show the gospel in its two directions: upward (prayer) and outward (mission), and the community of people in whom those directions are embodied.

The instructions on prayer and conduct (vv. 2–6) are brief but theologically dense. Prayer requires steadfastness and watchfulness — active, alert engagement rather than routine. Thanksgiving is its constant accompaniment. The prayer for open doors for the word of the mystery of Christ — the mystery Paul himself is imprisoned for proclaiming — is the prayer of a man for whom the gospel’s advance is more important than his own comfort or release. Conduct toward outsiders is to be “in wisdom,” making the best use of the time, with speech that is “gracious, seasoned with salt” — the attractive, preserving, flavour-giving quality that makes the gospel winsome as well as true.

The closing personal greetings reveal the extraordinary network of relationships through which the gospel was advancing in the first century: Tychicus, Onesimus, Aristarchus, Mark (the John Mark of Acts 15, apparently reconciled with Paul), Justus, Epaphras, Luke, Demas, Nympha and her house church, Archippus. These are not decorative biographical details; they are the human face of the gospel’s advance, the community of grace in its concrete, particular, named reality.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The instructions on prayer are brief but exact: continue steadfastly, keep alert, give thanks. The three qualities together describe a prayer life that is neither perfunctory (steadfast, not occasional) nor passive (alert, not sleepy) nor joyless (thankful, not merely dutiful). The specific prayer request Paul adds — for open doors for the word of the mystery of Christ — is remarkable for a man in prison: he is not asking for release but for continued opportunity to proclaim the message that put him there.

The instruction on conduct toward outsiders (v. 5) — walking in wisdom, making the best use of the time — reflects the eschatological urgency that runs through all of Paul’s letters: time is short, opportunity is limited, the gospel’s advance requires the community’s wise engagement with those outside it. The speech that is “gracious, seasoned with salt” (v. 6) describes the quality of Christian conversation: not bland and inoffensive (salt preserves and flavours), not harsh and alienating (seasoned, not overwhelming), but the kind of speech that creates appetite for the gospel rather than resistance to it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Prayer as Steadfast Engagement, Not Occasional Request

Paul’s instruction to “continue steadfastly in prayer” (proskartereite) reflects the Reformed conviction that prayer is not an emergency resort but the fundamental posture of the creature before the Creator. The same verb is used in Acts 1:14 of the disciples’ prayer in the upper room and in Acts 2:42 of the early church’s corporate life. Steadfast prayer is the mark of a community that has genuinely reckoned with its dependence on God and genuinely believes that prayer moves the hands that move the world.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul, in prison, could not personally open the doors for the gospel’s advance. He could pray — and he could enlist the Colossians to pray with him. The prayer for open doors is the prayer of the person who has surrendered control of the gospel’s advance to the one who actually controls it. Now: The church that wants to reach the lost but neglects corporate prayer has misunderstood the mechanism by which God works. Open doors are God’s to give; prayer is the community’s engagement with the God who gives them.

verseByVerse.quote: Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary: The household code that began with wives and husbands (3:18–19), children and fathers (3:20–21), and bondservants (3:22–25) closes here with masters — and the reversal is complete. The master who holds power over a bondservant stands himself under a Master in heaven, to whom he will give account for every act of injustice and unfairness. The word "justly" (to dikaion) and "fairly" (tēn isotēta) — equality, equity — set a standard far beyond Roman law required of slaveowners. The gospel does not immediately dissolve every social structure, but it plants within them a seed of equality before God that, properly cultivated, cannot leave those structures unchanged.

verseByVerse.quote: Continue steadfastly in prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving. At the same time, pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to declare the mystery of Christ, on account of which I am in prison — that I may make it clear, which is how I ought to speak.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Watchful in it” (grēgorountes) — alert, not drowsy. The image is of the soldier on night watch who cannot afford to sleep. Prayer requires the same quality of alert attention that all important things require: the mind genuinely present, genuinely directed toward God, genuinely expecting him to act. “A door for the word” — Paul’s metaphor of open and closed doors for gospel opportunity (also 1 Cor 16:9; 2 Cor 2:12) places the initiative with God: it is God who opens and closes doors; the apostle walks through the ones God opens. The mystery of Christ — for which Paul is imprisoned — is the same mystery of 1:27: Christ in you, the hope of glory. He is in prison precisely for proclaiming that the cosmic fullness of Christ is available to all people, without ethnic or ritual distinction. “That I may make it clear” — Paul’s prayer is not merely for opportunity but for clarity in the opportunity: the open door means nothing without clear proclamation of what lies on the other side.

verseByVerse.quote: Walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the best use of the time. Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Walk in wisdom toward outsiders” — the wisdom that governs the community’s engagement with those outside it is not strategy or technique but the wisdom of those who know the gospel’s truth and want others to know it too. “Making the best use of the time” (exagorazomenoi ton kairon) — redeeming the opportune moment, buying back the time that would otherwise be squandered. The “time” here is kairos — the decisive, opportune moment, not merely clock time. Every conversation with an outsider is a kairos, an opportunity that will not return. “Gracious, seasoned with salt” — the double quality of Christian speech: en chariti (in grace, graciously, attractively) and hērtymenos alati (seasoned with salt, preserving, flavour-giving). The gospel conversation should be winsome and substantive, attractive and truthful, neither insipid nor abrasive.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The letter closes with a remarkable catalogue of names and relationships: Tychicus, the letter-carrier, described as “a beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord”; Onesimus, “our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you” — the runaway slave of Philemon, now a trusted co-worker; Aristarchus, Paul’s fellow prisoner; Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, apparently restored to Paul’s confidence after the sharp disagreement of Acts 15; Justus; Epaphras, the founder of the Colossian church, “always struggling on your behalf in his prayers”; Luke the beloved physician; Demas (who will later desert Paul, 2 Tim 4:10); Nympha and the church in her house; and Archippus.

These names are the gospel in its concrete, human, particular form. The mystery of Christ — “Christ in you, the hope of glory” — is not abstract. It is Tychicus the letter-carrier, Onesimus the former slave, Luke the physician, Nympha the householder. The gospel that created the cosmos (1:15–20) arrives at these specific, named, loved people in these specific, named, messy situations. This is how the gospel has always advanced: through communities of named, particular, irreplaceable people who love and serve and pray and carry letters for one another.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Community of the Gospel as the Body of Christ

The list of names at the end of Colossians is the practical expression of the ecclesiology of 1:18: Christ is the head of the body, the church. The body is not an abstract entity; it is Tychicus and Onesimus and Luke and Nympha. The community of grace is always concrete, always named, always embodied in particular people with particular histories, gifts, and needs. Reformed ecclesiology has always insisted on the visible, particular, local church as the primary form of the body of Christ: not an ideal church somewhere, but this church, these people, this place, this time.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Onesimus is the most striking name on the list. The runaway slave, the subject of the letter to Philemon, is now a “faithful and beloved brother” being commended to the Colossians. The gospel has done exactly what Paul said it would do in 3:11: it has abolished the slave/free distinction as a defining category. Onesimus and Philemon are brothers; Onesimus and the Colossians are family. Now: The community of the gospel is always the community of the surprising, the reconciled, the transformed. The people who would never have been in the same room together are gathered at the same table because Christ is all, and in all.

verseByVerse.quote: Tychicus will tell you all about my activities. He is a beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord… and with him Onesimus, our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will tell you of everything that has taken place here… Aristarchus my fellow prisoner greets you, and Mark the cousin of Barnabas… and Jesus who is called Justus. These are the only men of the circumcision among my fellow workers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me.
verseByVerse.commentary: The tenderness of Paul’s descriptions of his co-workers is characteristic: “beloved brother,” “faithful minister,” “fellow servant,” “fellow prisoner,” “a comfort to me.” These are the relationships of the gospel community: not merely organizational colleagues but brothers and sisters in the deepest possible sense, sharing in the same mission, the same suffering, the same Lord. “Onesimus, who is one of you” — the Colossians know Onesimus; he is from their community. The runaway slave is now being sent back not merely to Philemon (as Paul’s letter to Philemon describes) but described publicly as a “faithful and beloved brother.” The social revolution of the gospel is being enacted in the act of commending him.

verseByVerse.quote: Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ Jesus, greets you, always struggling on your behalf in his prayers, that you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God… Luke the beloved physician greets you, as does Demas… Give my greetings to the brothers at Laodicea, and to Nympha and the church in her house… And say to Archippus, “See that you fulfill the ministry that you have received in the Lord.” I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. Remember my chains. Grace be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary: Epaphras, the founder of the Colossian church, is still “struggling” for them in prayer — the same word Paul used for his own struggle on their behalf (2:1). The prayer of Epaphras has a precise content: that the Colossians would “stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God.” This is the letter’s goal in miniature: maturity, not supplemented by esoteric knowledge, but the maturity of those who are fully assured in the will of God revealed in Christ. “Remember my chains” — Paul’s autographic note is both a claim to the letter’s authenticity and a reminder of the cost of the gospel he has been expounding. He is in chains for the mystery of Christ. The letter they are reading was written by a man in prison. “Grace be with you” — as in Philippians, the first word is also the last: grace, the free, inexhaustible, sovereign gift of God in Jesus Christ, in whom the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and in whom you have been filled.
